subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to make statutory provision for foreign exchange control now exercised- under the authority of orders in council passed under the War Measures Act and for that purpose, inter alia, to (a) continue the special exchange fund account in the name of the Minister of Finance established under the Exchange Fund Act; (b) establish a foreign exchange control board which will be the successor of the existing foreign exchange control board and have power, under the direction and control of the Minister of Finance, to regulate and control transactions in foreign currencies and related transactions and to manage and operate the exchange fund account; (c) authorize the Minister of Finance to make advances to the exchange fund account out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may prescribe; (d) authorize the payment out of the exchange fund account of such remuneration to authorized dealers as the governor in council may prescribe.

subtopic: MOULDERS' STRIKE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA- REPRESENTATIONS OP ENGINEERING FIRMS
speechtext: I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Labour. subtopic: MOULDERS' STRIKE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA- REPRESENTATIONS OP ENGINEERING FIRMS
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to send me notice of his question. The wartime labour relations regulations, P.C. 1003, are administered in British Columbia by the Minister of Labour for British Columbia. That was the original arrangement when the regulations were drafted. As a consequence, all industrial disputes in that province are dealt with by the conciliation service of the province except those which are ordinarily within the legislative authority of parliament, such as disputes affecting railways, navigation or shipping, and by arrangement disputes affecting the coal mining industry. The foundry dispute is being handled by the provincial department of labour.
Mr. MacINNIS1: May I ask a supplementary question? Has the minister been advised by the premier of British Columbia or by any official, that they consider this a matter that comes under the federal department of labour?

subtopic: MOULDERS' STRIKE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA- REPRESENTATIONS OP ENGINEERING FIRMS
speechtext: I have no knowledge of that. I believe the statement I have made is a fairly practical one. It is obvious that the federal department of labour cannot get into every dispute in every province. subtopic: ALLOCATION AND DISPOSITION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLOCATION AND DISPOSITION
speechtext: I sent the Minister of Veterans Affairs notice of a question, but I see he is not here. Since the question has to do with the three defence departments, I will ask that it be taken as notice. Has the government complied with the recommendations contained in the fourth report of the canteen committee, which was set up in 1942, to arrange machinery for the allocation and disposition of canteen funds accumulated during the war?

speakeroldname: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ALLOCATION AND DISPOSITION
speechtext: Perhaps I might answer that question now. We are giving careful consideration to the whole question of canteen funds. I have asked the officers of my department to get me certain information in connection with them. Although I will not make any positive statement to this effect, I think I shall wish to suggest that at the next session of parliament we set up another committee on canteen funds, because the question is an important one. My present view is that it would be well to have the question considered by a committee of this house, but I do not think it would be possible to do it at this session. subtopic: STEPS TO FACILITATE TRANSPORT OF FIANCEES TO CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: STEPS TO FACILITATE TRANSPORT OF FIANCEES TO CANADA
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Mines and Resources in his capacity as Minister of Immigration. On behalf of a number of Canadian

servicemen who have fiancees in Holland, Belgium, France or other European countries, may I ask the minister whether he will try to find a way to facilitate their coming to Canada at an early date? Is it possible to give these girls the same consideration as that given to overseas war brides?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: STEPS TO FACILITATE TRANSPORT OF FIANCEES TO CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member gave me notice of this question. The problem of the movement to Canada from the continent of Europe of the fiancees of Canadian servicemen is primarily one of transportation. A similar situation exists in the British isles, where many fiancees are awaiting an opportunity to proceed to Canada to join their intended husbands. It is not possible to make provision for the movement of fiancees on the same basis as the wives and children of servicemen. There are still approximately 25,000 servicemen's wives and children in the British isles, and 2,400 on the continent. These are being brought forward just as quickly as transportation is available and they are, of course, entitled to preference.
I can assure the hon. member that everything possible will be done to facilitate the movement of servicemen's fiancees. The situation is a difficult one. There are still many Canadians overseas who have been waiting for many months to secure accommodation for return to Canada; in fact some of them have been endeavouring to return since early last year. There will, of course, be an immediate improvement in the situation when the movement to Canada of service personnel and their dependents is completed.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, June 11, consideration in committee of bill No. 165, relating to the development and control of atomic energy-Mr. Howe-Mr. Macdonald, (Brantford City) in the chair.
On Section 1-short title.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
Press dispatches of this morning indicate that the United States government has released information about the use of atomic energy. Can the minister give a statement to the committee telling us just what the United States action means?
Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply); I am afraid I did not read the article. I saw the headlines and intended to read it, but I have not had time; therefore I cannot answer the question.

Atomic Energy Control
I know of no special release of information about atomic energy, although there very well may have been such a release. Canada, in any event, was not consulted in the matter.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
Can the minister indicate
what the expenditures in connection with atomic energy control will be during the fiscal year? I notice that in Great Britain an estimate was given when their bill was introduced into the House of Commons. The Canadian ministry must have some idea as to what the cost will be.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: So far as the current fiscal year is concerned, there are two types of expenditure involved, one on capital account and the other on operating account. At the moment the two pretty well overlap, because there is still some work going on in construction, and also some on operation. The construction of the Chalk River project will entail a cost of about $20,000,000. I am not sure how much will be spent this year; perhaps it will be five or six millions, which will be a carry-over from last year

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: The total capital expenditure on Chalk River will be $20,000,000?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Yes. The operating is estimated to cost $3,500,000 annually.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Are there any other expenses involved in addition to those at Chalk River.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: No, not directly on atomic energy. At the moment the activities of the Eldorado company are self-supporting, and I know of no expenditures outside of those I have mentioned.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Definitions.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: This is the section which deals with various definitions. For example, it defines the board, the president of the board, and a member of the board. Has any consideration been given to having the minister, who is over the board, a member of the board itself? It does seem to me that there might be some merit in having a member of the government an actual member of the board. It would tie the House of Commons in that much closer with the activities of the board.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
I suggest that it would not be good organization. I think the board should have some body capable of sitting outside its orbit to review its work. For example, in my department the deputy minister is never permitted to be a member of a board of directors, the theory being that the job 63260-157J
of the deputy minister is to see that the work of the board is kept in order. I rather think there should be a wholly outside body to check this work. If the minister was on the board there would be no one except parliament, or the government as a whole, perhaps, to check the work of the board.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Order. May I point out to the committee that we are now dealing with the definitions. Section 4 of the bill sets forth the composition of the board. Probably this discussion would be more appropriate under section 4.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Section 2 defines a member, the board and the president. Surely we are in order in asking questions such as I asked on this section; and I think we will get along a great deal faster if we are not tied down too rigidly on the sections. I believe my question was quite in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I am not saying it is not in order, but I should think any discussion as to who sits on the board should be taken up when we are considering the composition of the board. I thought it would facilitate the work of the committee if we discussed that matter when discussing the composition of the board. However, I am entirely in the hands of the committee.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I want to ask the minister if he believes the rule-and I consider it a good rule-which precludes deputy ministers from sitting on the board of a crown company would necessarily apply to a minister. It seems to me that it would be a proper thing to have the minister on the board, because the company is administering and spending crown moneys. With the minister on the board the house could feel that it had a watch-dog on the board, and it would have a representative responsible to the house whose presence on the board would do away with much of the criticism that has been levelled at crown companies in that they are spending money without control on the part of the house.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the objection to having a deputy minister as a member of the board would apply with even greater force to the minister himself. After all, this board reports to a committee of the privy council, of which the minister is chairman. I never think it is very good organization, though many people would disagree with me, to have the president of a company act also as general manager. I believe the management should be separate, in a sense, from the policy-making branch, so that there may be a check on the manage-
Atomic Energy Control

ment without the policy-making body necessarily becoming part of the technique of management.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I do not want to press the argument unduly, but I submit that while the theory to which the minister has just given expression may be good in business, there is a difference between ordinary procedure in business and the procedure which should be followed when crown moneys are involved. Does he not feel that a distinction should be made where a crown company is spending crown moneys; would it not give parliament more security and the government a better opportunity to maintain control of the moneys spent if it were represented on the boards of these companies?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: It occurs to me that there would be two or three objections. For example, sitting on a board of five the minister might be overruled and outvoted four to one, which would hardly be consistent with the line of authority. Then if a recommendation came from a board of which the minister was a member and it became the duty of the deputy minister to overrule the decision of the board, or to recommend to the minister that he overrule that decision, there would be some difficulty. I am strongly of the opinion that the board will function very much better if no minister of the crown is a member of it.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Would that difficulty be overcome if provision were made in the bill that the minister be an ex-officio member of the board? That would give him the right to sit in at any time.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: He would still be a member of the board, and I think the same objection would apply.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: If the minister has some direct tie-up with the board it brings parliament that much closer to it. As the minister knows, in the United Kingdom the minister of supply is the whole board; there is no one else. Everything is handled directly under voe minister. Perhaps we could get around the difficulty in the way I suggest.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
I would call my hon. friend's attention to section 7 of the bill, which reads:
The board shall comply with any general or special direction given by the committee-
That is the committee of the cabinet.
-with reference to the carrying qut of its purposes and shall advise the committee on all matters relating to atomic energy which, in the opinion of the board, may affect the public interest.

In other words it is a board under the minister and subject to direction by the minister. I have never found that boards exceed their authority in spending money. The boards with which I am familiar have been most careful to make sure a project is approved before any expenditure is undertaken. The fact that the minister can change the personnel of the board at will, and the fact that the board must be subject to a specific direction if the minister gives it, I think set up a relationship better than would result if the minister were to act as one of the five members of the board itself.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
Section 2(a) provides:
"Atomic energy" means all energy of whatever type derived from or created by the transmutation of atoms.
In his able address on June 3 the minister mentioned the possibility of this energy being applied to civilian pursuits for the benefit of mankind, and he referred particularly to heat. The cost of producing this energy will be so prohibitive that in my opinion it will never be used to furnish heat and for other social and civilian purposes. The other day I quoted authorities to support this opinion. Electrical energy in Ontario, which in 1923 amounted to one million horsepower, at that time was the equivalent of twelve million tons of coal. I believe we have some 47,000,000 horse-power in Canada, only one-sixth of which has been developed for the benefit of the cities, towns and farms of this country. The atom will never accomplish anything like that. Fancy that, Mr. Chairman; in your own province the electrical horse-power developed in 1923 was the equivalent of 12,000,000 tons of coal. The other day I quoted the opinions of two of the greatest scientists in the world to-day on the cost and distribution of atomic energy. As you know, after every war some new invention comes along which causes people to have fabulous dreams of big things which, when examined from the scientific standpoint, do not measure up. If atomic energy would do anything comparable with what electrical energy has done in taking the place of coal, then we would have something to look forward to. The cost of using the atom to produce heat and the cost of transmitting that heat would be prohibitive.
There are other matters dealt with in section 2 to which I referred the other day. I do hope the real men of science will be in charge, not just gentlemen who may be presidents of universities, with administrative power, but men who know something about science itself. It is only in the last ninety years (hat science has discovered the power

Atomic Energy Control
inherent in coal, oil and falling water, and the great benefits resulting therefrom to mankind. Those three discoveries did more for science than any other agencies. After all is said and done, in the last ninety years science has won the admiration of the world. It argues from facts, realities and examinations. It makes discoveries after taking great pains, with care and toil. The work of many thousands is devoted to science; they are the missionaries carrying on their explorations for the benefit of mankind.
Science is not like politics, or some other branches of endeavour. It is not always up in the clouds; rather it argues from facts. If the atom can be developed as a producer of power, as have coal, oil and falling water, it will be worth while. I am very very doubtful, however, about that development because, as I said the other day, sometimes we have on these scientific research boards men who are just executives and who have no knowledge of science. They are appointed because they may have been the heads of some department or other. I should hope that the board would consist of Canadians, because people in this country have shown that they are second to none in scientific endeavour.
From his experience in this connection, I believe the minister knows more on this subject than most of us in the house. I do suggest to him that any development of atomic power, while commercially costly, would most certainly be an important factor in a country such as Canada which requires heat for ten months of the year. Does he hope that from atomic energy heat will be developed, as it has been from the other discoveries I have mentioned, so as to relieve the people of this country from much of the cost involved in heating houses, hospitals and other buildings? Does the minister hope that the very laudable object mentioned in his speech of June 3 will be attained?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I am hopeful that means will be found to convert atomic energy into usable heat at reasonable cost. When one stops to consider that a person could put enough plutonium in a capsule the size of a fountain pen to drive a battleship around the oceans for three years, it seems conceivable that means can be found to make use of atomic energy as valuable to the world as is the use of electricity at the present time.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
A few minutes ago the minister referred to a committee of the cabinet to which the atomic energy control board will report, of which committee I believe he said he was chairman. Who are the other
members? I suggest it would be particularly desirable to have the Minister of National Defence a member of that committee.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
As I said the other day, the committee consists of the following:	The
Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, chairman; the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Mines and Resources, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Labour.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I note there is a definition of the expression "prescribed substances." It is my understanding that wide powers are taken to deal with the production and use of prescribed substances.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
The definition reads:
"Prescribed substances" means uranium, thorium, plutonium, neptunium, deuterium, their respective derivatives and compounds and any other substances which the board may by regulation made under this act designate as being capable of releasing atomic energy, or as being requisite for the production, use or application of atomic energy.
Those last few words would seem to be wide indeed, because there must be many substances which could be regarded as requisite for the production, use or application of atomic energy. Is it necessary to have a definition as wide as that? Are the last two lines required?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: We are only at the beginning of the age of atomic energy. At the present time the only element capable of setting up chain reaction is uranium. Uranium is the heaviest of the elements. The next heaviest is thorium. While it is not believed at the present time that chain reaction can be set up with thorium, it may be used to supplement uranium by using the two together. It is quite possible that improved methods of setting up chain reaction will be found, and that the metals lower in the scale of the elements may be used. Therefore it is felt the board should have power to extend the list of metals over which it may exercise control, as the advance of science may indicate.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
Yes, but the words to which I have referred go much farther than the matter of defining substances. They cover articles used in the production of atomic energy. For instance, those words could be construed as being applicable to machinery, and many other articles. I refer in particular only to the words "or as being requisite for the production, use or application of atomic energy."
Atomic Energy Control

It may be necessary to have those words, but it seems to me there is a question whether the definition is too broad.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I have no doubt the hon. member has the British act, which is considerably broader than ours. That act says that a "prescribed substance" shall mean uranium, thorium, plutonium, neptunium, or any of their respective compounds, or any such other substance as the minister may by order prescribe, being a substance which in his opinion is or may be used for the production or use of atomic energy, or research in matters connected therewith. The United States act contains a broader definition than this measure does. I suggest this provision is no wider than may be required to meet further developments. I can assure the hon. member that the board will not take action in respect of a substance unless it can prove to the minister, and through him to the house, that such action is justified.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Board constituted.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
While section 3 makes the atomic energy control board a body corporate, and gives it the right to contract in the name of His Majesty, and to acquire property, it does not contain any provision that such body corporate may sue or be sued. I suggest that in that respect it is out of line with the policy we have heard enunciated in recent days. Of course we are not dealing with companies which may be set up by the board; but when the board itself is a body corporate, one would think the same principle ought to be adhered to.
In bill 155, respecting the operation of government companies, there is provision in section 7 under which every company may sue and be sued in respect of any right acquired or obligation incurred by it, as agent of His Majesty. It is true that the atomic energy control board is not to be a joint stock company; it is to be a body corporate, and it would seem only reasonable and logical that the same principle should be applied, that it may sue or be sued.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that we are not organizing a business; we are organizing a corporation to deal with atomic energy. It is intended that that corporation shall have the same immunities as the crown in acting for the crown in connection with that subject. I have suggested to the house on several occasions that if the board intends to do business, for instance if it intends to run Chalk River as a business institution, a company will be set up under the Companies
fMr. Green.]
Act which would not enjoy these immunities. This is simply to give the board a corporate identity with immunities similar to those enjoyed by the crown.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I do not think the situation is completely covered by the minister's answer. It may be intended at the moment that the actual transacting of business in respect to the development of atomic energy shall be carried on by companies to be set up under a later section. Under section 3 certain powers are being conferred upon this board, which is to be a body corporate. Situations may arise which we cannot foresee at the moment, where the board would have dealings with individuals out of which contractual rights would arise. Section 3 provides that the board may contract in the name of His Majesty and that property acquired by the board shall be the property of His Majesty, but a situation might conceivably arise in which persons would acquire contractual rights against the board, and it would be a hardship to compel such persons to apply for a petition of right to' sue the corporation. If we recognize the principle that business is to be carried on through a corporation, we should recognize the principle that such corporations should be able to sue and be subject to being sued.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: I should like to supplement the questions put by the hon. member for Eglinton by referring the minister to section 8, subsection (h), which seems to contemplate the actual carrying on of business and which would seem to be in line with what the hon. member for Eglinton has said about the impropriety of there being immunity.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Section 3 indicates that the atomic energy control board can act only as the agent of His Majesty, and that the powers exercised by it shall be exercised only as an agent of His Majesty.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Is not that true of all crown companies?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: They are not restricted.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
That is provided in the bill
we passed the other day.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
I would refer the minister to section 7 of the bill we passed the other day respecting the operation of government companies. It reads:
7.	(1) Every company is for all its purposes an agent of His Majesty and its powers may be exercised only as an agent of His Majesty.

Atomic Energy Control
(2) Every company may on behalf of His Majesty contract in its corporate name without specific reference to His Majesty.
The minister's answer may have reference to the second subsection, but the first subsection makes it quite clear that every one of the companies set up under that bill, or under the research council act, shall act as agents of His Majesty.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: A corporation set up under the Companies Act contracts in its own name, whereas this board will be able to contract only as an agent of His Majesty. In other words, if it buys land, it will buy it in the name of His Majesty, and the land will be registered in the name of His Majesty. There would seem to be no purpose and every reason against putting in a provision that this board may sue or be sued.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Would it not be a corollary that there is nothing in this act which does apply to the carrying on of business or which empowers the board to carry on business in the ordinary course of events?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Under section 9 the board is to make regulations for developing, controlling, supervising and licensing the production, application and use of atomic energy. It has power to regulate those matters, but those are not matters of business. They are matters for the crown, and in carrying out its duties the board will be acting only as the crown. Would it not be better to discuss these matters under the proper sections? It is hard to jump back and forth.

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext: Section 3 is the one that provides for setting up the board. It seems to me that some consideration should be given to having an advisory committee, such as I referred to the other day when we were discussing the bill on second reading. When the minister closed the debate on the second reading he did not deal with the advisory board that is to be set up in the United States. They are to have an honorary board of nine members, presumably scientists or manufacturers, which will check the activities of the atomic energy control commission. Could not something of that type be set up here? The other night the minister told us that perhaps in time it would be well to have a committee of the house check the activities of our atomic energy control board, but how about an advisory board made up of civilians?

subtopic: PUBLIC CONTROL AND SUPERVISION OF DEVELOPMENT, APPLICATION AND USE
speechtext:
It will be remembered that the atomic energy control commission in the United States will take over more than two billion dollars' worth of property. They are to, take over a going concern which is spread over a great deal of territory. The position
here is quite different. We are setting up our board at the inception of the development, and there would seem to be no purpose in having an advisory committee. It will be difficult enough to get five men who can make any real contribution at this time, and I would not know where we could get nine more. While consideration has been given to the matter, the decision has been taken that at the present time, rather than having an advisory committee, the board will report to a cabinet committee.

212. Civil service health division (including medical investigation division), $180,078.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Under this item, the services for which the minister intends to provide, as outlined by him at page 3608 of Hansard of the previous session, are covered by a six-point programme. The minister referred to the fact that in May, 1945, he was authorized by the government to announce a programme involving an expenditure of $328,000 for the first year to provide a number of health services for civil servants. The six-point programme mentioned by the minister was to cover: (1) Examination before entrance into the civil service, including X-ray for tuberculosis; (2) periodical examinations; (3) emergency service; (4) educational facilities; (5) advice; and (6) the establishment of sanitary standards. The item approved at the previous session called for an expenditure of $145,750. I do not recall whether there was a supplementary estimate in connection with the item, but the item now before us involves $180,078, and we are shown the same figure as having been appropriated in the preceding year.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When the civil service health programme was approved by the governor in council in May, 1945, as the hon. member said, and as I mentioned last week, the estimated cost of providing full service for one year was, as I intimated, $328,000. It was not found possible to inaugurate the programme in full and it is not yet in operation in several important respects. Our inability to put it into effect has been due to shortage of doctors and dentists, shortage of nurses and shortage of space. These shortages are being gradually overcome and the programme is now being carried more fully into effect. I described it last session, and I do not propose to take the time of the committee to-night in going over again the objects of the programme in detail.
Generally speaking, it aimed at giving a health service comparable, if not superior to that generally in force among the employees of leading employers. We had in mind the services provided by the Canadian National
Supply-Health and Welfare

Railways, the Bell Telephone company, the Metropolitan Life Insurance company and other large employers who had instituted services of this kind and who, we were informed -investigation proved this to be the case- had found that these services not only improved the health of the employees but also improved employer-employee relationships. It was demonstrated in other cases that the cost of the service was more than met out of the savings in illness, premature retirement, sick leave and the like.
As hon. members no doubt know, there has been a serious shortage of doctors in Canada, since so many were engaged in war services, and every public health service and every community are consequently suffering from the shortage. The same is true of this department; and it has not been possible for that reason, as well as because of the shortage of space, to implement the programme more fully. I may tell the committee, however, that there already was a health service provided for civil servants in Ottawa under which X-rays were taken; and a very large proportion of the civil servants in this city were examined in the year 1943-44. In consequence of that, a number of cases of active tuberculosis were discovered; a number of persons were hospitalized, and the results obtained have more than justified expenditures.
In addition, at that time-the same is true to-day-civil servants on becoming permanent were required to be examined; and also, in connection with retirement and sick leave, examinations were undertaken by the medical investigation division of the department. That division really laid the foundations for the more ample service that we are now giving. The service, we hope, will be centred in the offices ,in the Jackson building where the department's headquarters are now situated.
We hope there will be health units in a number of office buildings in different sections of the city where there are large numbers of civil servants, and there will be preliminary examinations on entrance and regular laboratory tests, medical advice and emergency service. There will also be a programme of health education which will be an important feature of this service. Altogether it is expected that with the return and discharge of members of the armed forces who are in medical, nursing and dental professions, it will be possible to bring this rapidly into effect by stages in the different buildings in which we hope to establish units.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This is an item in which the amount asked for this year is $6,000 less than what was asked for last year. If I may say so, I am sorry to note that reduction because it seems to me that it might turn out that there is nothing more important in the field of national health than nutrition. I notice in the details given on page 164 of the main estimates that, although there may be some explanation which the minister can give for it, the top person listed in this division is a grade 2 stenographer. That is hardly good enough for nutrition. Perhaps in the temporary assistants' item there may be amounts for the employment of people of a little higher grade. But I want to impress upon the minister my feeling-and I think it is shared by a good many-that this is a field in which research ought to be done, and in which all possible information should be got out amongst our people.
The idea that care of our health consists not only in curative and corrective measures but also in preventive efforts is now pretty well established. When we stop to think of it I believe we all recognize that if we are to encourage preventive attempts to improve our national health, probably this is the place where we shall have to do some real work, namely in connection with the whole question of nutrition and diet. I think it must be admitted that even though there is the will to eat according to the best ideas of the correct diet we do not yet know what is the best diet for the human body. I was interested in a press dispatch which appeared in the newspapers earlier to-day, to which reference was made this afternoon, about developments in connection with atomic energy. In that dispatch it was suggested that very soon it would be possible, because of the research being done in atomic energy, to learn more about the chemistry of the human body, what it does with medicines that are given to it and what it does with food, so that possibly we may be on the threshold of new discoveries and greater knowledge about the effect on our national health of nutrition, diet and the foods we eat from infancy throughout the whole of life. Therefore I would urge most strongly that in this field the minister not pay too much attention to those who are trying to pinch pennies here and there. I urge that he fight within the cabinet and treasury board for all the money he can get for this kind of work.
While I am referring to the importance of nutrition as far as research, knowledge, publicity and information are concerned, I hope there will be no request for this item to be cut down, because I want to see it extended. But I think one must also tell the minister again what has been said to him a number of times on this subject, that it is not enough just to find out what is the proper diet, to give publicity and information in regard thereto, and to ask the people to eat the best foods, if at the same time the government takes off the subsidy so that the price of milk goes up, fails to give old age pensioners adequate allowances, and so on. I suggest that it is part of the minister's job, as guardian of the national health, to fight for measures on the part of the government to which he belongs which will make it possible for people to get the foods which, nutritionally, are best for them. This is really something pretty basic, pretty fundamental
Supply-Health and Welfare

to the health of our people. Not only is that so with respect to the generation now living in Canada, but it is also possible that if we really put some effort and research and money into this subject we may receive the thanks of two or three generations ahead, if by having done so we find ways and means of so feeding ourselves that we become a healthier and happier race of people.
My tune, as the minister recognizes, is a little different from that which he hears from some hon. members with respect to these estimates. I regret that there has been a reduction this year in this item, and I should be glad to hear what plans the department has in the field of nutrition service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on the importance of this subject. The reduction in the estimates-which is not very great, amounting to $6,039-is due entirely to an adjustment with regard to the amounts provided for temporary assistance and cost of living bonus. If the hon. member will look at the estimates for 1945-46 and* compare them with the estimates for 1944-45 he will see that there was a considerable increase as between those two years. As a matter of fact they went up from $63,181 to $149,031. Our experience during the year has shown that we can make this adjustment without impairing the service.
With regard to the type of work done by the division, it includes research activities, including dietary and nutrition service and tabulations. There we work closely with the provinces, and at the request of provincial health authorities have made surveys of a considerable number of places. Surveys are being carried on to bring to light nutritional deficiencies due to one reason or another so that proper nutritional standards may be built up. The work also includes education with regard to nutrition, both through contacts with the provinces and communities and through various media. These include the use of films; wall charts, which are distributed wholesale and are colourful and useful with regard to diets; small sheets that were distributed on street cars and which had a general distribution; a wide range of pamphlets, and posters. The division also gives advice on group feeding in connection with quantity food services to industries, camps, small hospitals and so on. An active correspondence is carried on and a considerable amount of field work is done. Finally, the division works closely with other agencies of the government, as, for example, the armed

forces, veterans affairs and others, in seeing to it that as far as possible the nutritional standards of the country are built up.
It is common knowledge that during the war the nutrition of the Canadian people was greatly improved, partly due to higher take-home wages, partly due to improved knowledge, and partly due to the development of good nutritional practices in industries and other places where groups of people were fed. We hope that work will be continued and extended. We find there is a great deal of room for work in marginal areas, as, for example, in the far north with our Eskimo and Indian people, and in various parts of Canada where nutritional standards are not as high as they should be. We hope to continue along that line, working closely with the provinces and any other agencies engaged in that field.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This department is labelled the Department of National Health and Welfare but, so far as making any contribution to nutrition is concerned, the department is doing nothing that I know of. They have a national health department in Great Britain, and what do they do? They provide meals for the underprivileged children in the schools. What are we doing over here? We have a skeleton department that spends $11,000,000 on public health and which used to spend only $500,000 before the war. All they do is to give advice to the provinces and municipalities regarding public health.
I read a letter in the Globe and Mail this morning criticizing one of the officers of the department because he was travelling all over the world giving advice. They must have an awful lot to do here in Ottawa in the national public health department when they can find time to take trains and planes all over the civilized world. Planes here and planes there, hotel bills everywhere; they have a staff travelling along, secretaries and a whole retinue; almost a small standing army. When the war started and so many men were overseas the municipalities were faced with the necessity of setting up day nurseries to take care of the children in those families where the mothers had to go to work because they did not have enough money to pay the rent. These day nurseries were opened up and the children were taken in and given milk and food. What are we doing? We are spending money to visit security councils when there is no security at all in any land.
The first thing I want to know is: What does a lawyer know about nutrition? Why should a lawyer be heading the Department of National Health and Welfare? When I was chairman of the board of health I had one of the greatest health officers at the head of the department, Doctor Hastings. He knew the whole business from top to bottom. If the government is not prepared to do the right thing, let us abolish the department altogether. They are doing nothing for national health. What has happened to the nurseries which were opened in order to provide hundreds of children with a little bit of lunch when their fathers and mothers were out working? They closed them up. They told the municipalities that that item would be struck out of the estimates, but yet they find money with which to visit New York and travel all over the United States taking up all the hotel space and the reservations on planes. These are the wonderful people who are doing so much for public health.

As far as I can see, the department is doing nothing. All that they do is give advice to the municipalities. I receive their literature but I just throw it in the wastepaper basket because it would be a waste of time to read it. The writers do not know very much about public health and yet they clutter up the mails with all this stuff. If the government want to do something they should do what they are doing in Great Britain. Some of the officers of the department have just come back from the United States. They cannot see a day wasted without visiting Washington, Chicago, Buffalo, Cleveland and New York- all aboard! The whole staff are ready to go to make some investigation or inquiry into public health and make speeches in the United States. What do they care about the children in our public and separate and other schools of the country who cannot get milk, with the two-cent subsidy now cut off? There are a great many of these children in my own constituency. They had a school down at Little Norway. They cannot get houses, they cannot get homes; they cannot get anything. Yet all we have is this skeleton department giving advice to the municipal health officers.
A lot of the health officers are getting pretty sick of it. I was talking to three or four of them about it the other day, and they wanted to know what I was going to do to try to get this item for the day nurseries back in the estimates. Many of these men know more about public health than some of the fellows I have seen in the department. If we are to have a national health department, let us have a good one. Health is the most important thing that I know of. Some of those who have been in this parliament have gone because they could not stand the pace. If we are going to do something for public health let us find the money to do it with. It is the duty of the government to look after the peace, health, comfort and prosperity of its people. Do you think visiting the United States will help the children of this country?
Nothing has been done at all. No houses, no homes, no food, no milk, no day nurseries. All they need is one or two cents for milk to provide the necessary nutrition, and yet they are ready to spend thousands of dollars in carrying on a useles advertising campaign. I often pity the taxpayers of the countiy. Fortunately there is an election every year in municipalities and here every five years, and the government will have to answer when they are asked: What are you doing for public health? What are you doing for consumption? What are you doing about heart diseases? What are you doing about cancer? One of the finest members of the house suffered from
that dread malady. It is just like Santa Claus; one of the officials of the department said that there was no Santa Claus, and there is no Santa Claus as far as this department goes. The municipalities have to be the Santa Claus. They have to provide the funds for real public health.
We spend more money on education in one year than they are spending. Here we are spending 811,000,000 on a skeleton health department of talk. We spend from $12,000,000 to $13,000,000 a year on educating our children. These day nurseries are needed and we should have visiting nurses who could go to the homes of these poor people who are living down in the cellars and all that kind of thing. It is a good thing that we have had the school system we have because the children can at least go to school and be warm in the day time. Some of the schools are beginning to give meals, but they are getting no help from Ottawa.
Ontario is the forgotten province. There has been no cabinet minister from the Toronto district since 1935. Yet there are one, two, three, four, five or six from Montreal. The time is coming when we should either have a real national health department that can provide nutrition and all the rest of it, or we should have no department at all. It is time the government cut out a lot of this waste and duplication. I know the young minister is not to blame for all this because he took charge of the department just at the time of the baby bonus. But I think it would be far better to give bonuses, subsidies and subventions to municipalities to build and maintain hospitals, and liberal grants for cancer, heart disease, consumption, than to spend money the way it has been spent by the government in the past on a national health department that is merely national in name and gives only advice.

Items 214, 215 and 216 relate to the combating of venereal diseases, and perhaps what I have to say now will apply to all three. The first item is administration, $36,000 roughly; the second is assistance to the provinces for control of venereal diseases under regulations approved by the governor in council, $175,000; and the third is distribution of drugs under regulations approved by the governor in council, $50,000.
Supply-Health and Welfare

The first two represent reductions from last year's estimates; the third item is the same as last year's.
In all fairness to the work of the department under this branch, it should be observed that the actual administration of methods of combating venereal disease must fall under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and the contribution of the dominion in this field cannot in peace time be as great as in war time. There was a great opportunity during the war for the dominion, through this department and its predecessor, to take effective measures on various fronts to combat the spread of venereal disease. It requires no further words on my part to establish the seriousness of the whole problem. It is a serious problem in this country; but it is one which, by enlightened methods, can be reduced in its scope if, indeed, it cannot be overcome.
The effect of remedial measures of the right kind is shown by the reduction in the incidence of venereal diseases in the armed forces during the war, by methods carried on under dominion jurisdiction. The report of the department for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1945, at page 62, gives certain figures showing the reduction in incidence in the disease in the armed forces, beginning with the year 1940 and ending with 1944. Statistics for 1945 are not available to us. In the navy the rate per 1,000 in 1940 was 58; in 1941 it rose to 60, and from that point on it was reduced until in 1944 it was 32, which is less than 50 per cent of the incidence of venereal disease in 1941. In the army the incidence of the disease reached its peak in 1940, with 62 per 1,000 in that.year. It was reduced each year until in 1944 it had been reduced to 29, less than half of the rate of incidence which prevailed in 1940. In the air force in' 1940 the rate of incidence was 29, and it was reduced in each year until in 1944 it was 18 per 1,000. These figures are most significant in showing what can be done by effective measures. Of course it is not possible to take measures with reference to the civilian population in the same way as it is possible with reference to the armed forces. There are not the same opportunities for inspection and control, but there are important lessons to be derived from the experience of Canada in time of war in seeking to combat the incidence of venereal disease in the armed forces.
In a review of this particular item in the estimates of the department last year, the minister outlined a programme on four fronts. His remarks are to be found at page 3600 of Hansard of December 15, 1945. He spoke about a series of advertisements issued by

the department emphasizing a four-sector front against venereal disease. These four sectors of the front are health, welfare, legal and moral. If the minister will be so kind I should like him to outline what programme his department proposes to follow this year with reference to this problem, bearing in mind, of course, the constitutional limitations on the powers of the department. In particular, I should like to ask him what measures the dominion hopes to initiate or bring about by education or other methods on the moral front? I am moved to say this, not with a view of repeating what has been discussed more than once in this chamber, but because I think it has a direct bearing on any measures that this department proposes to take to combat venereal disease on the moral front. I am sure that we must put far more emphasis on the moral attack on venereal disease than has been done hitherto.
The deputy minister of this department on the health side has made certain public statements, and I should like the view of the minister in regard to the relation of some of the statements of his deputy to the efforts of the department to combat venereal disease on the moral front. Doctor Chisholm's opinions are his own business; but the statements which he makes in his capacity as deputy minister of national health in the time of the department, the time of the people of Canada, are, I think, a matter of genuine Concern to the members of this committee. When Doctor Chisholm speaks in public on these matters, undoubtedly he is recognized as speaking in his capacity of deputy minister of national health, and his remarks must certainly be construed by the public as having some relationship to the policy of this department.
In all fairness, I say that there has been a good deal of misapprehension about the remarks of Doctor Chisholm. There has been so much publicity given to his remarks on the subject of education of children, on the subject of Santa Claus, that some of his remarks which are of greater significance have been lost sight of. What I am speaking of to-night has nothing to do with Doctor Chisholm's views on the matter of instructing children in regard to Santa Claus. His remarks which I shall quote relate directly to what may or may not be the policy of this department in attacking venereal disease on the moral front. I shall quote the exact words used by Doctor Chisholm in his lectures at the William Alanson White memorial lectures in the United States last fall. This is what he said:
Is there any force so potent and so pervasive that it can do all -these things in all civilizations?

Supply-Health and Welfare
He was dealing with the question of inferiority, guilt and fear and the effect of these things in controlling people's actions and inhibitions. I continue:
There is-just one. The only lowest common denominator of all civilizations and the only psychological force capable of producing these perversions is morality, the concept of right and wrong, the poison long ago described and warned against as "the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil."
In the old Hebrew story God warns the first man and woman to have nothing to with good and evil. It is interesting to note that as long ago as that, "good" is recognized as just as great a menace as "evil." They are the fruit of the one tree and are different aspects of the same thing.
We have been very slow to rediscover this truth and to recognize the unnecessary and artificially imposed inferiority, guilt and fear, commonly known as sin, under which we have almost all laboured and which produces so much of the social maladjustment and unhappiness in the world. For many generations wre have bowed our necks to the yoke of the conviction of sin. We have swallowed all manner of poisonous certainties fed us by our parents, our Sunday and day school teachers, our politicians, our priests, our newspapers and others with a vested interest in controlling us. "Thou shalt become as gods, knowing good and evil," good and evil with which to keep children under control, with which to prevent free thinking, with which to impose local and familial and national loyalties and with which to blind children to their glorious intellectual heritage. Misguided by authoritarian dogma, bound by exclusive faith, stunted by inculcated loyalty, torn by frantic heresy, bedevilled by insistent schism, drugged by ecstatic experience, confused by conflicting certainty, bewildered by invented mystery, and loaded down by the weight of guilt and fear engendered by its own original promises, the unfortunate human race, deprived by these incubi of its only defences and its only reasons for striving, its reasoning power and its natural capacity to enjoy the satisfaction of its natural urges, struggles along under its ghastly self-imposed burden. The results, the inevitable results, are frustration, inferiority, neurosis and inability to enjoy living, to reason clearly or to make a world fit to live in.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have listened to what the hon. member has read. What does Doctor Chisholm really mean?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should have thought the pith of the remarks of the deputy minister is that the heart of our problem is that we choose to recognize such things as good and evil. His argument here is that the cause of our troubles is the conception of morality which rests on religion and the religious conception of good and evil; therefore he says, do away with that and a lot of your trouble will be over. Further on in his address, he says:
Freedom from moralities means freedom to observe, to think and behave sensibly, to the advantage of the person and of the group, free from outmoded types of loyalties and from the magic fears of our ancestors.
The committee is entitled to know whether that represents the type of attack which this department conceives to be the proper type of attack on the problem of venereal disease on the moral front. I suggest that when we are called upon to vote substantial sums of money to assist this department in combating this dreadful venereal disease; when it is recognized by the minister himself that it has to be attacked on four fronts, not the least of which is the moral front, we want some positive assurance from the minister that statements of this type are disclaimed by the department as representing the policy and view of the department. In the second place, we want an assurance that it is not going to be countenanced by the department on the part of a civil servant, speaking in his capacity as a civil servant, in time paid for by the department. If the deputy minister is to continue in office, and I take it he is since this matter was touched upon last fall, we want some assurance that remarks of this kind will not be made by him in his official capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon member for Eglinton has raised, this question and I am very glad to reply to him. In the first place, I should say that Doctor Chisholm is a doctor and scientist of considerable distinction who during the war rendered great service as director general of medical services of Canada, during the very period when this reduction in venereal disease was effected and when the front against venereal disease included the moral front. He was selected to come to this department and was appointed on the recommendation of the Prime Minister in November, 1944, and he has given great service in organizing the department. When he delivered the speech in Washington just referred to he was speaking as a professional man to an audience of professional men. In no wav did he represent himself as speaking for the department or the government of Canada. Incidentally, not that it matters so much, he spoke when he was on leave from the department, his first leave since joining it.
I do not intend to go over the ground covered in the speech to which the hon. member has referred, or what has been quoted by my hon. friend. Nor do I intend to try to explain what Doctor Chisholm meant in the words he used. But I think, if the speech is read as a whole, its general purpose will be seen. It is this: that because of his experiences in two wars, because of his knowledge as a scientist, Doctor Chisholm, like a great number of other people in the world, including the present Prime Minister in speeches in this house, has reached the strong conviction
Supply-Health and Welfare

that unless mankind does something to look after its own affairs better than has been done in the past we are likely to have another war which will destroy a very large proportion of civilization, if not mankind itself. That, I think, is clear from this speech and other utterances of Doctor Chisholm, as well as of other people. Holding that view as strongly as he does, he finds that the trouble lies in ourselves, and he suggests some remedies, some changes in attitude.
Certainly I do not pretend for a moment that the views he expresses are my views. I believe, however, that he has sincerely stated his views because of his strong convictions, and has stated them in all sincerity as an approach to the settlement of the question of war and peace, of man controlling himself as well as his environment. The object. I think, is to try to get people to think for themselves. I have discussed this matter witn Doctor Chisholm, as hon. members may imagine, and from that discussion I personally do not think one would find anything in what he said which was an attack on morality in any proper sense, or on a proper concept of good and evil, or on any religion. That is the impression he left with me in the discussions I have had with him.
It is quite obvious that in this he was not speaking for the department or the government. I think it is equally obvious from his whole record that he is a man of great sincerity and deep personal conviction. When as deputy minister of the department he supports and , in fact directs a campaign against venereal disease, which includes an attack on the moral front, he means that; and it is an important element in the attack on venereal disease, as the publicity and educational activities of the department have pointed out and as the hon. member for Eglinton has said. It is mentioned fourth in - the list for reasons of climax, as being the most important element in it. The publicity issued, either through films, posters, pamphlets or newspaper advertisements, all emphasizes this; and I can assure the hon. member that as long as I have anything to do with the department they will continue to emphasize it.
The campaign to which he referred and the programme about which he desired information is being carried on largely in cooperation with those agencies throughout the dominion which are directly engaged in dealing with the problem. Within the last two months there was held in Ottawa a meeting at which the venereal disease enforcement officers of the various provinces and others representing the armed forces discussed further plans and

agreed on a common line of attack. Among the most important things are the distribution of infomation, the cooperation with regard to statistics, and also the possible development of common lines of attack through action in the courts and otherwise, as well as in the all-important field of education. All that activity is being carried on in cooperation with those agencies, in the directions that were outlined previously.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then might I ask the minister the reason for this great reduction in the amount for publicity and information in the estimates for 1946-47?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The reason for the reduction is the relatively large item which was included in the estimates for the previous year to cover the cost of a campaign that was carried on during the month of November. 1944. That campaign included a large amount of newspaper and other kinds of publicity. It received general commendation and was useful, but it is not the kind of thing we would wish to repeat every year. It was done in conjunction with the war, and also in conjunction with a similar campaign being carried on in the United States. The possibility of holding another campaign will be under consideration, but it is not contemplated for this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I congratulate the hon. member for Lanark upon his drawing attention to the serious implications of venereal disease. At the same time, however, I would question the consistency of several of his colleagues who have been attacking the ministers, including the one now before the committee, for too heavy expenditures on publicity. I believe that inconsistency should be explained, because [DOT]on the one hand we cannot have increased expenditures for some worth-while form of publicity, and decreased expenditures on the other. I believe it was the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who on June 7, as reported at page 2314 of Hansard, referred to this specific appropriation.
I note that in connection with venereal diseases there is an appropriation to the provinces. Why is it constitutionally sound to make additional grants to the provinces for the control of venereal diseases, for physical fitness programmes, but constitutionally unsound to make a grant in connection with the nutritional matter of supplying milk for school *children, which I mentioned a minute ago. It was pointed out that such additional grant was ultra vires or unconstitutional. What is the explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Replying to the hon. member for Lanark, might I point out that under the next item, 215, there is included in the sum of $175,000 an amount of $25,250 for
education in connection with venereal disease.
Then, replying to the hon. member for Regina City, I could, as I have said, discuss at some length the constitutional question. Offhand I would say, however, that whereas it would be possible for the federal government to make additional grants in aid to the provinces for purposes such as this, and to make them constitutionally and practically, I fail to see how we can make available to the provinces for payment to individuals throughout the provinces moneys for the purpose he has mentioned. I should think that kind of payment would lead to all kinds of constitutional and administrative difficulties.
It seems to me that there is a fundamental difference, and that the answer we have given is the right one, namely that the right way to deal with such a matter is by general arrangement to put the provinces in a position where they can discharge their own responsibilities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There is no hint in anything I have said that additional grants made by the Canadian government should not be to the provinces in the nature of grants for milk for school children. The details could be worked out, if the approach were properly made in the form of an offer from this government. We have made a much greater grant by way of family allowances. We are told that in the next year it will amount to $250 million. It seems that the expenditure depends on what the grant is to be made for. It seems to me that the minister is not logical in what he says.
I approve entirely the principle of a grant to fight venereal diseases, a grant for a national physical fitness programme, and for payment of family allowances, and hope that the list can be extended, because it is only in that way that we can equalize opportunities as between the wealthier and poorer individuals. It seems to me that the minister has not fully answered my question as to the constitutional difficulties.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What I have to say relates specifically to item 215, wherein it is indicated that grants to provinces for assistance in the control of venereal disease have been reduced by $33,000. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext:
Will those be made available to the committee before we complete these estimates? As I said before, in 1919 the dominion government undertook a policy of making grants to the provinces. In order to qualify, a province had to establish free clinics, free hospital beds for indoor patients, provide treatment to gaol inmates, appoint a specially trained director, all of which was subject to inspection by a federal official. In 1919 the total grant was $180,000. By 1922, all the provinces with the exception of Prince Edward Island had qualified by meeting the conditions I have just stated, If I may repeat, in 1932 the grant was eliminated.
The provinces were left in this position, which has happened in connection with so many federal grants. They were encouraged to establish machinery to meet certain conditions and they banked upon the grant made by the dominion only to find, after the machinery was functioning and could not possibly be done away with-the people demand these services-that the dominion was withdrawing from the field and leaving the provinces to bear the full burden of the cost.
There should not be any reduction this year, next year or the year following in the grants to provinces to assist in the control of venereal disease, unless at the same time it can be said that venereal disease has been wiped out entirely in this country. I realize that health is primarily a responsibility of the provinces; but we have just come through a national tragedy, namely, a war, and we have had to face abnormal conditions in connection with these diseases. Since people migrated from one section of the country to another this has really become substantially a federal responsibility. Let me emphasize what I said a moment ago. I trust that there will be no attempt made, no matter what demands for economy are put forth, to eliminate this fed-
[Mr. Claxton.l
eral grant to assist in the control of venereal disease, unless it can be said that veneral dis-' ease no longer exists in this land.

speechtext: I should like to refer back to the remarks made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Regina City and assure him there is no inconsistency as far as this group is concerned. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I expected that the hon. member for Eglinton would follow up his attack on the moral aspect of this venereal disease question, but he appears not to be intending to do that. I find myself somewhat confused by the whole situation. I am not able to gather w-hat the minister conceives to be the moral attack on venereal disease.
I could understand his conceiving venereal disease to be the result of a lack of morality in the country and that lack of morality to be owing to a lack of faith in religion and in God and his undertaking to use a method of attack through an educational campaign that would restore the belief of the people in God and Christianity and thereby make the people sense their responsibility to God a little more and refrain from the offences which result in venereal disease.
I can understand some such line of attack as that being a moral attack on the problem, but I must say that apparently the minister has left unsaid the very things that he needed to have said in order that I would be able to see how the speech of Doctor Chisholm, which the hon. member for Eglinton quoted, could have anything to do with the moral attack on the venereal disease question. Perhaps the minister can elucidate the matter for me. I have three questions to ask which will probably assist him.
The first one is: What does the minister mean by a moral attack on the venereal disease problem? Second, does the minister conceive Doctor Chisholm's remarks, as quoted by the hon. member for Eglinton, to be a contribution to the attack on venereal disease on the moral front? Third, the minister has said that Doctor Chisholm is a great scientist; what bearing on the moral aspect of the attack on venereal disease does the minister conceive that fact to have? If the

Supply-Health and Welfare
minister will explain that I probably can get myself correctly orientated in regard to this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am not prepared to develop for the benefit of the hon. member for Lethbridge-

speechtext: Why not include the committee?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is not a sufficient answer. If a moral attack on venereal disease means anything, it means a moral attack. If remarks are made in the country which tend to destroy the faith of the people in God, in Christianity and in the moral standards which we have had for generations; if those things are being done in a public way and the faith of the people being destroyed, I fail utterly to see how a moral attack is being made on the venereal disease question. I believe a good deal of explanation is due the committee. I represent a constituency in which this is a serious matter, and I believe that a good many hon. members do.
