maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am not at all satisfied about this matter. I think the people of Canada are entitled to a clear statement as to the significance of some of the speeches that have been made by the deputy minister of health. He might have been speaking in an unofficial capacity, and in so far as he was doing so, well and good. I am not particularly criticizing that gentleman. I am criticizing more the attitude which is being adopted by a good many men who call themselves scientists and who assume things that have never been proved and then proceed to make a great many remarks based on their 63260-160
false assumptions and spread them abroad all over the country, tending to destroy the faith of the people.
My judgment is this. At least I am inclined to believe that there is a lot in this, that the venereal disease which has developed in this country has developed as a result of a deliberate propaganda which has been going on now for something like two generations and which is aimed at the destruction of the faith of the people. I had the privilege of going to university, commencing in 1909 and going on to 1913, and what went on in that university was a long, long way from anything that would be conducive to the building up of faith in God. About all that we were taught faith in was evolution. I have an idea that that sort of thing is going on in most of the universities in this land. Certainly it is being propagated in a good many textbooks and in many of the illustrated lectures and in slides. If this sort of thing goes on throughout the country and no attempt is made on the part of Canada as a whole to offset that tendency, we are just throwing good money down the drain when we attempt to cope with venereal disease.
I do not suppose that hon. members will accept this as a particular authority, but I happen to have in my hand a statement by Henry Ward Beecher, which is of interest in this connection. He says: "Morality without religion has no roots." I am inclined to think that philosophy is just about right. "Morality without religion has no roots."
I said the other day, on June 7, that I believed the people had to return to God, and I think that is one of the very first things to do if we are to make an attack on venereal disease on the moral front. If we do not do that, we are not attacking venereal disease on the moral front.
The minister will remember that on June 7 I asked a number of questions designed to bring out the number of films which were being shown by the national film board and which tended to indoctrinate evolution. I do not know whether the minister has had time to get the answers to questions, I asked that day, but if he has, I should like to have him give the answers now. I asked another set of questions on that same day designed to give him an opportunity of telling how many films the national film board is showing which are designed to increase faith in the bible. If he can tell us that I shall be glad. If we find that there are a good many films tending to establish the evolution concept and very few films tending to establish faith in the bible concept, we can get a pretty

Supply-Health and Welfare

good idea of what the minister and his department mean by	a moral	attack	on
venereal disease.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better
deal with the hon. member's question with regard to the film board, although it is totally	irrelevant to this item,	by saying
that when the item comes before us I am prepared to deal fully with it. I do not know of any film such as he has in mind.
With	regard to his	question	about	themoral front and various other fronts in attacking venereal disease, it is quite obvious that we are doing the job of combating venereal disease	through various	agencies	which	are
appropriate for each part of the job. With regard to health, that is done through the weapons of modern science, making treatment available, educating people to look after themselves, public health procedure.
Mr. BLACIvMORE:	That would be the
intellectual front, not the moral front.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
1N0; that is the health
front.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That is intellectual.
You would not call that moral.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
On the health front you find physicians, health nurses, university medical training centres, hospitals, free treatment centres and so on. On the welfare front are the people who work to improve living conditions, social workers, welfare agencies and all the other instruments used to combat squalor and overcrowding, bad sanitation, neglect and insecurity.
On the legal front the aim is to conduct a vigorous, unrelenting and sustained attack in the courts, through the use of the machinery of the courts, and police agencies whose job is to seek out and bring to justice those who for personal gain cater to man's weaknesses. On all these different fronts the agencies appropriate to each are the ones to take action. On the moral front the battle is led by the churches and by the homes of Canada. They work together to inculcate a moral attitude and uphold the sanctity of marriage and of family life.	[DOT]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
If that is the meaning of "moral" I believe that every member of this committee will agree that anything that tends to establish the evolutionary theory or the higher criticism attitude toward the bible or to undermine belief in God, Christ or the bible is diametrically opposed to every one of the elements working in the interests of the moral life of the country, because they are opposed to those elements which are working [Mr. Blackmore.j
for the establishment of spirituality in the country. I do not wish to labour this point. I believe that there should be a united effort from coast to coast in this country among the people, not among the lawmakers, to reestablish faith in God, faith in the bible, faith in Christianity and to offset the pernicious effects of the evolutionary theory. The evolutionary theory was never more than a theory and, as the days go by, it is being shown more and more to be unfounded in fact. Why, then, should we have our films filled with it, our textbooks filled with it, our university courses filled with it? It is a problem the people must deal with, and as a member of this house I suggest that the people from coast to coast take this matter with great seriousness.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member for Lanark has correctly described the purpose of the division. It was created in consequence of a resolution passed at a meeting of the dominion council of health held in May, 1945. That council consists of the deputy ministers of health of the dominion and the provinces and some laymen. The resolution recommended that this department be established and devolped to provide a special service for the purpose of advising the provinces in respect of the planning and building of modern, practical and reasonably priced public institutions including tuberculosis, mental, convalescent, and general hospitals and public health and other clinics, old age homes and so forth, to collect and tabulate and make available all the latest information on the subject, to be prepared to study problems of construction, and to advise on the planning of buildings and the development of minimum standards as a guide for future types of public institutions. That is a very large programme, and it is intended to achieve this through the appointment, which has been made, of a well-qualified architect. He will also concern himself with 63260-160J
the development of plans for the department's own hospitals, advise the other departments of the federal government with regard to hospital design, equip himself by looking at hospitals that have already been built, of different types in different parts of Canada, the United States and other countries; and otherwise acquire the knowledge necessary to develop standard types of design and specifications for different sizes and different types of hospitals. These will then be available to any province or municipality or private hospital which desires to build in order to put their plans and specifications in the hands of their own architect, thus enabling him to start with something from which he can work in order to meet the needs of the particular type of hospital and locality concerned. It will be a free service to facilitate the design and construction of hospitals in the various communities. It is important because it is estimated that to fill the needs of Canada there will have to be an amount ranging from $125 million to $200 million of hospital construction over the next ten years. It is thought that this service will be of use in that connection,

speechtext:
Then what I was informed was correct. I shall re-read (d):
That the services to combat the problem are inadequate.
I am going to deal with each one of these items, but not from any knowledge I have. I was very happy to read almost a complete description of these four headings in the Toronto Star of last evening. Here is what the Star said in an editorial:
A third of all discharges from the armed forces in Canada were due to psychiatric disabilities.
That bears out what I have been told by Doctor Hincks.
Over ten million persons in the United States require hospitalization for mental illness, but adequate institutions are not available.
[Mr. Claxton.l
That bears out heading (b). I am not reading these remarks consecutively as they are written in the Star, but consecutively to suit the headings I have before me. I continue:
It is deplorable that known methods for the cure and prevention of mental disease are not being applied on an adequate scale. Hospitals for mental disorders are many of them understaffed, overcrowded, ill-equipped and in old buildings unsuitable for modern therapy.
In one year the minister, of course, has not had time to overcome such a big problem; but . I am glad to know that the programme is greatly expanding and is to be greatly enlarged. I continue with the Star's editorial:
If the curative and preventive measures developed during the war were applied many now in hospitals might be restored to normal society; many more might be prevented from requiring institutional care.
When I visited that hospital some few weeks ago I had no notion that mental hygiene was of such importance, or that our mental problem was of such a magnitude. In this connection I read to-day an article entitled "The Problem of Prison After-Care," by J. Alex. Edmison, K.C., executive secretary, prisoners' rehabilitation society of Ontario. In the article I found some interesting figures which bear out what I have already said. The article states:
In the annual report upon the prisons and reformatories of the province of Ontario for 1945 it was shown that during the year 2,810 inmates had been in the Ontario reformatory at Guelph. Of these 10-13 per cent were mental defectives . . .
I am glad the Minister of Justice is in his seat because I shall likely be repeating some of this material when his estimates are up for consideration, particularly in connection with the matter he referred to last year on prison reform. I continue:
Of these 10-13 per cent were mental defectives, 14-04 per cent were borderline, 32-79 per cent dull normal.
The evidence from the prison bears out what I read in the Toronto Star article and supports the four headings into which I divided the remarks of Doctor Hincks.
I am happy to notice that this item has been increased. I trust that the programme the minister has in mind will be greatly expanded and that this disease which appears to be a great scourge, something which I had not known of before, or that we had such a great percentage of people who are mental defectives, will be vigorously attacked. I remember what Doctor Hincks said, namely, that if the disease could be caught when people are young the effect of it in after years could be greatly

Supply-Health and Welfare
overcome if not wholly eliminated. Therefore I wish to repeat that this item has my undivided support.
I know nothing whatever about medicine. I am sure the hon. member for Lanark could give a much clearer talk on this subject than I can. I am happy to know that the hon. member for Lanark is a medical man. I am pleased to note that every time he speaks in the house the press gives him wide publicity because they know that he knows what he is talking about. I was also glad to note what the hon. member for Broadview said this evening. He is modest in his statements; but I know that the hon. member for Broadview, who was the mayor of Toronto for seven terms, was the father of the well-known, highly-commended medical department of the city of Toronto. I believe he was responsible for urging the late Doctor Hastings to become the head of that department, and everybody knows that Doctor Hastings did a good job.
I wish to compliment Doctor Hincks who, as I have, learned from other sources, devotes his entire time to this work, but not for the remuneration that he gets out of it. I was told by a gentleman who was well acquainted with him that Doctor Hincks was offered a large salary to go to New York and carry on mental hygiene work there, but being a Canadian and a lover of the great city in which he lives he decided to concentrate his life's work to that city. I am sure that the minister knows about that great work. I have heard Doctor Hincks speak very highly of the minister. He has a splendid board supporting him. The president of that board is a man whose name has been mentioned earlier this evening,' Major General G. Brock Chisholm. The vice-president is Sir Ellsworth Flavelle, bart. The treasurers are Philip S. Fisher and Fred Page Higgins; the latter is the only one I know, and he is an estimable man. The scientific adviser is Professor D. Ewen Cameron. The medical director is Doctor J. D. Griffin, and there is a long list of eminent men who are directors, whose names I shall not take time to read. Perhaps I should mention one who is no doubt, well known to the minister, Mr. Morris W. Wilson, C.M.G., chairman, who I believe, lives in Montreal. The list also includes Mr. Norman J. Dawes, Mr. William F. Angus, and quite a number of others, including Doctor F. Cyril James.
That is all I have to say about this matter. As I said a moment ago, personally I know nothing about it, but I became enthusiastic by what I heard, and I was greatly pleased with the improvement in the health of the person I went to the psychiatric hospital to see. If the psychiatric hospital can do that
sort of work, can bring about a restoration such as I saw in the person I went to see, a person well up in years, I have a pretty clear conception of what can be done if this type of illness is treated in time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Ontario, in common with the other provinces, takes care of its own mental cases. While it is true there is a shortage of beds for mental cases in this province, still it is a fact that psychiatry is really a new science, and a large percentage of the people going into these mental institutions are cured. They are not called crazy people any more. It is recognized now that people can suffer from mental illness as well as from any other kind of illness. I should like, however, to ask a question of the minister, in view of the fact that the care of mental cases falls on the provinces. Of what benefit will be this amount of $32,000? How is it to be expended by the dominion government in connection with mental illness?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The purpose is to make available to the provinces, the municipalities and local institutions technical advice on matters of mental health. The chief of the division is to give a series of lectures to public health institutes, doctors, nurses and so on. Already he has given those lectures in British Columbia, where he gave a two-day institute for workers in Vancouver. The division is to act as a clearing house for the provinces in matters of professional information and to provide them with information as to the availability of personnel for all classes of mental health work. A directory is being prepared. Tire division will plan, in consultation with the provinces, adequate preventive measures and treatment facilities. It will stimulate parent education across the country by making available literature and other educational material to direct the attention of parents to the advisability of seeing to it that the mental health of their children is looked after as well as their physical health. It will carry on the education of the public. It will encourage research in the field of mental health.
This is not designed to be in any sense a large division. It will have a chief and a clerical staff, and I think that is all. Just one doctor will be available in the way I have described. The situation with respect to mental - health is described at some length in the green book, the reference paper, "Health, Welfare and Labour," where full statistics are given showing the incidence of these conditions across Canada and the need for a great deal more work in this field. The proposals of the dominion government
Supply-Health and Welfare

did include a substantial grant for mental health among the health grants which were proposed, which was to be increased to a total of $6,000,000 a year distributed among the provinces in accordance with population. That was to be a conditional grant. This division will work closely with the Canadian council on mental hygiene, to which the hon. member for Davenport referred.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am still not clear on the
tie-up with the provinces. Since they produce their own personnel for the hospitals, and the psychiatrists, I am not clear on the part played by this division in giving advice on matters of mental hygiene.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I thought I gave a full
answer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There was just the one point, about giving advice to the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The director will be
available to give advice. Already in one case, that of British Columbia, he has given a course of lectures on this subject, and I think that illustrates the way in which he will be available. The division will also act in the interchange of information between the provinces, so that they may exchange professional and technical information and information as to personnel.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Following up that point,
did any of the provinces request that this service be provided? As I understand it, this dominion service is of recent origin. How did it come about? Was it at the concerted request of the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In this sense only, that in 1944 the provinces were called into consultation in regard to the health insurance bill then being considered by the social security committee, and that bill provided for health grants, including the mental health grant to which I have referred. After spending three days in Ottawa, the representatives of the provinces made a number of suggestions with regard to those proposals, and then it was understood that they agreed to them. It was quite obvious that the federal government could not arrive at a plan for the distribution of any such sum as four or five, six or seven million dollars to assist in mental health work unless it had its own professional adviser in that field; and at that time the question of such an appointment was considered. As far as I know, that is the only way the provinces might have known this appointment was under way. I think it was implied in the extent of the project which was under discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would it be correct to understand that an attempt is made to avoid duplication of expert opinion? Is there an attempt by the dominion to get experts of different kinds who will not be in any way duplicating the provincial work, so that it might be considered an addition to the field; or might one find there is duplication?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think I can assure the hon. member that there is no duplication; that the functions we have in mind for the various divisions of the department involve no duplication whatever. The various divisions are charged with the work of securing the interchange of information between the provinces. Attached to almost every division in the department there is an interprovincial committee or a committee of professional experts with representatives from each province. In that way the divisions of the federal government provide machinery whereby views are interchanged and plans are coordinated. I have not known of any case in which there has been any duplication at all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then is it quite clear that the dominion has become a sort of channel of communication between the provinces, and that the provinces find it more convenient to communicate with each other through the dominion than directly; or are there two parallel lines of communication?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The fact is that through these agencies such as the dominion council on health, the Canadian council on nutrition, the national physical fitness council, the advisory committees to the division of food and drugs, the conference of workers on venereal disease, people from the provinces meet at Ottawa, exchange views, receive information and give advice. That is the way in which a large part of the work of the department is carried on. That is, we are in (communication with them and they are in communication with us. Then the representatives of the provinces or of professional associations meet at Ottawa and exchange views. It is the best way we know of in which the work in different fields can be coordinated throughout Canada. But it is largely the result of consultation and discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I do not know whether the same condition applies throughout Canada, but in most county homes I believe at least a third of the cases could be classified as bordering on mental. Is any assistance given in that regard?

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No assistance is given by the dominion. That was the kind of assistance contemplated in the dominion government's proposals under which grants totalling S7 million might be made, for assistance in providing care for mental cases. That money would have been paid to the provinces, and distributed through various types of institutions within those provinces. But at present there is no such provision.

Item agreed to.
National health branch-
221.	Blindness control division, $42,566.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This item contemplates an increase from $10,520 to $42,566. What expansion in programme will there be?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The largest single item is an increase of $19,000 to cover the cost of medical specialists' fees in connection with a survey of blind pensioners, together with the cost of treatment of some of those pensioners whose vision may be benefited by medical or surgical procedure as indicated by the findings of the survey. This is part of a programme we have set under way, under which we hope to find out what proportion of blindness can be prevented or cured by treatment.
In the proposals to the provinces we offered to contribute 50 per cent of the cost of providing treatment, where that treatment might result in preventing or curing blindness, by operation or other means. As it is, we are going to continue the survey so as to find out the causes of blindness, what proportion can be treated, and carry on some test work to see how much it will cost to do a really big job in that field, with the hope of reducing the number of blind people from the substantial number there are in Canada to-day. It is believed that expenditures by the dominion and the provinces on this work would ultimately result in a reduction in the amount of pensions payable to blind persons.
. Mr. FLEMING: Will that survey involve original research work? Will that not be done in provincial institutions? We are concerned lest the programme contemplated by the minister's department might result in a duplication of the work now being carried on. How will the proposed expansion of expenditures under the item meet a need not at present being met by work done by the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I believe it is correct to say that at present no one is charged with finding out from medical files what the causes of blindness are, from a statistical point of view. This is largely a statistical operation, but it must be done by doctors. It is believed
that this is the only way in which the information can be obtained. The work was started some time ago, and this is for an extension of that work. We hope through this means- the only means we know of-to find out all there is to know about causes of blindness in Canada, and to estimate what proportion might be cured by treatment or operation. This is not a duplication of work being carried on anywhere.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is the work being done by persons on the staff of the department, or are expert research workers being retained for the purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not think the expression "research workers" would be exact.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Statisticians, then.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This $19,000 additional is to provide payment to specialists who will do the survey work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Specialists outside the department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are six items in the division, and I am not objecting to any of them, because in my view the work supposed to be done is most desirable. The point raised by the hon. member for Eglinton is worthy of consideration. Is there cooperation between the minister's department and the various provincial departments in these matters, or are they matters which are outside provincial departments altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The situation is that of the 12,652 known blind people in Canada, some 6,882 were on pension as of January 1, 1946. We have records in the old age pensions office relative to each of those pensioners. Our aim is to go over those records, and also to go over the records of other agencies to find out the causes of blindness in Canada. There is no duplication in the work.

Item agreed to.
National health branch-
222.	Tuberculosis control division, $32,051.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I do not rise to criticize the minister, but rather to appeal to him for support. I was sorry that the dominion-provincial conference failed, because I had hoped that we would receive from that conference some support in the control of this terrible scourge which sweeps the country.
In Manitoba one person dies each twenty-four hours from tuberculosis. That is a heavy deathrate. I have told the house before just how bad it is. When we send tuberculosis-
2ozti
Supply-Health and Welfare

tested cows to the north country we find that the people give the cows the disease before they are there three months. That is how bad the condition is. I have read in the newspapers where this matter has been discussed by provincial governments, but we find that very little has been done for the control of the disease.
I am pleased to note that another $15,000 is being set aside for that purpose. However, that is not nearly enough. The disease in the northern part of my constituency is spreading like wildfire. I know of one poll consisting of 120 voters. There are about 200 people in the settlement, and it was found that of that number there were seventy-two people infected with tuberculosis. There were twenty-one at home. At the last report eleven were active and probably would require treatment; three needed further investigation and eighteen were reported as having communicable diseases. When you have seventy-two out of 200 people in one little settlement in this condition you can realize how serious it is. This matter was brought up in the Manitoba provincial house by Mr. Hamilton, who represents a northern constituency, and Mr. Richards, but they do not seem to be able to do anything. This is a matter for the dominion to tackle. The dominion will have to step in and do something about it.
I do not want the committee to think I am speaking only about Indians because this is a mixed population. I hope something will be done, because people who go up there and work come back and find that there is something wrong with them. It is so easy to get this disease. I appeal to the minister to try to provide more money to control this disease in the north country, because it is worse there than in the southern parts of the province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the minister upon increasing the amount being made available to deal with this scourge of tuberculosis. We have been fighting tuberculosis quite successfully in the province from which I come. Of course, we have no monopoly upon what we are doing, since this is general throughout the country.
I wanted to speak about something not altogether connected with the disease. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister certain privileges which are denied to people confined in sanitaria. I refer to the exercise of the franchise. Prior to the last dominion election this caused considerable trouble in my constituency. The electoral act does not appear to be clear on the matter, and the electoral officers at that particular time seemed
FMr. Bryce.]	I
unable to give a clear definition of the act. As I say, they did not seem to be sure on the matter, and the information we received at different times prior to the election was quite conflicting. As I understand the act, it provides that people in charitable institutions-I want to protest now against the use of that word-and inmates of sanitaria were to be deprived of the right to vote. As I contended when dealing with citizenship, the right to vote should be irrevocable, and I want to protest as forcibly as I can against the disenfranchisement of anyone unfortunate enough to be afflicted with tuberculosis.
We attempted to have the inmates of a sanitarium in my city enfranchised. We wired the electoral officer several times, and finally we were told that only those who had been in residence for a period of twelve months and had no hope of getting back to their constituencies could vote. We thought that was perfectly clear and we rejoiced when the telegram came through, but it is a sad commentary upon the stupidity of some of the returning officers in this country when I say that they interpreted that to mean that only those could vote who had been in residence for a period of twelve months and were considered to be incurable. After further wiring, we were able to change their minds, and we were permitted to take those people out to vote who had been certified by the doctors to be able to go.
Tuberculosis is not like other diseases and that is one reason why those patients who have been certified by the doctors to be able to do so should be able to go out to vote. I appeal to the minister to use his influence in this, particular matter. I see no reason why the electoral act should not be amended to permit or even to compel the setting up of polling booths in these institutions, so that the inmates could vote without sacrificing their comfort or running the risk of aggravating their condition.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I notice that we have the same situation here as existed in connection with the other matter. When I was discussing the matter of research in tuberculosis two or three weeks ago I got into an argument with the hon. member for Mackenzie. I have here a copy of my local paper, the Perth Courier, and the editor has plastered the whole front page with the statement that free tuberculosis clinics are being provided. That is what is being done in Ontario, and they are doing the same thing in Saskatchewan. I cannot see why $32,000 is necessary when the provinces have control of their own tuberculosis campaigns and their own sanitaria.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The answer I would give to the hon. member for Lanark is exactly the same answer that I made with regard to mental health. The relation of the medical officer to be appointed with respect to tuberculosis is the same as the relation of the medical officer appointed with regard to mental hygiene. The positions are exactly the same; the divisions set up are similar, and the provisions for salaries are the same.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the medical officer consult with the Ontario department of health? Would he go out to the Lady Grey or up to the Muskoka sanitarium in order to give advice?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: He would if he were called in, and he would also be available in connection with work in other provinces. It is easy for any persons coming from Ontario to feel that they are able to look after their own health matters. That is so to a marked degree, but the same situation does not apply in some of the other provinces wThere the need with respect to certain diseases is much greater than that of Ontario. None of these officers would do work on patients in a province, but they would be available to work with the province in a consultative capacity.

Item agreed to.
National health branch-
223.	Advertising and labels division, $70,463.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In this item we have an increase from $13,000 to $70,000. Would the minister indicate just what the programme is that *would justify this increase in expenditure?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would allow the minister to tell us just what this item covers, just what this branch of his department does? Perhaps the hon. member for Eglinton knows, but I must plead ignorance and I should like to have the minister explain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The Food and Drugs Act is one of the oldest acts dealing with any matter affecting health which the department has to administer. It antedates confederation. There are extensive provisions in the act to protect the public against fraud and against injury to health, and not only for maintaining a service to ensure the purity of food and drugs but also to review the labelling and advertising of food and drugs. There are provisions in the act and in the regulations made in consequence of the act requiring that all packaged food and drugs be labelled and their contents be shown. These provisions are
enforced by the enforcement officers of the division. There is also a considerable amount of work involved in ensuring that the advertising matter does not make unjust or unfair claims. That requires close cooperation with those engaged in the production of food and drugs, and with advertising agencies and others who have to deal with advertising.
This division also reviews all radio scripts advertising food or drugs. It makes the cases on which prosecutions under the Food and Drugs Act for contraventions in respect to labelling and advertising are instituted. During the last year it has been working at a code which it is proposed to discuss with those engaged in the trade, in the hope that they will largely enforce this. It is also assembling a series of administrative decisions on the use that may be made of various words and so as to establish uniform practices by those who want to advertise.
The division has hitherto operated under two or three different branches of the department. Those have been assembled this year in one division, known as the advertising and labels division. That is the reason for the increase. There is also an increase in salaries-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You mean that the $13,000 shown for last year is not strictly comparable with the range of work covered by the $70,000 for this year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is right, but I should add that there is a considerable increase in the provision for salaries, with additional staff.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister has already pointed out that this thing has been going on for many years now, and we like to think that the work has been conducted reasonably efficiently up to the present time. I was going to ask, therefore, why the item has gone up six times, but that question is not applicable after what the minister has just said. It would, however, be well to know just why it has gone up, and to have figures which are comparable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I will repeat that this division is brought into existence through the assembly in one division of work that has hitherto been carried in various divisions. The first vote that was ever made to this division was $13,000. That was in the supple-mentaries for last year, but it represents only a portion of the year's work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I do not quite understand. Why are we not given the whole picture? Let me make this comment. I do not want to appear to be quibbling, but we should all face the fact
Supply-Health and Welfare

that when you set up a new department you set up a new kingdom, and a lot of people are continually wanting to extend that kingdom. While these are small amounts, nevertheless we should have a look at them and make sure that we are getting value for these items, and the only way in which we can make sure is to have the figures presented in such a way that we can make a strict comparison and know exactly what is going on. As the hon. member for Vancouver East said the other evening-and I considered it wise- these discussions either mean something or they do not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall be glad to get the information for the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The columns of figures showing the expenditures for last year and this ought to be as strictly comparable as they can be made. From what the minister has just said, these are not strictly comparable so far as this particular item is concerned, and wherever that occurs I think a detailed explanation ought to be made by the minister. Otherwise the comparison set out in the two columns is of no value to us. Where the two columns are not strictly comparable, the first explanation the minister should make is that they are not comparable and are not intended to be. If the different ministers have submitted their estimates in this way I think they ought to look over the figures that have been given to us for, as one hon. member said, either they mean something or they do not. This particular comparison is valueless.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Hon. members must recognize that when a new department is formed and takes over the functions of an old department and fits them into the work of the new department, necessary adjustments must be made as it is established. When we planned the work of the department in October, 1944, it was without any administrative staff, and it was not until March 31, 1945, that we were able to establish separate books and begin our own operations. Then the estimates came on in November, 1945, before there was a fully developed administrative staff and before we had had even one full year's operating experience. In view of that, some adjustments were necessary, and these adjustments I am ready to explain. I have answered every question that has been put and I shall be glad to answer any other questions. The item before us is due to the fact that the work which it is proposed to carry on under the advertising and labels division was hitherto carried on by the dominion analyst as part of his functions and with his office and by the director of
public health service as part of his functions and with his staff. It was found that the work had developed, and there were complaints from the trade with regard to the efficiency and fairness of administration and the speed with which answers were given. It was felt that it was necessary to establish a new division and this vote is put in for the first time to do that. The explanation that I gave before, that the only time the vote appeared was in the supplementary estimates, being $13,000, is quite correct. If there are any items which appear in this vote of $70,463, which were taken out of the votes for other divisions and appeared under other columns in previous estimates, I shall be glad to let the leader of the opposition know, or on the other hand I shall let him know if this represents an entirely new expenditure over and above the $13,000 put into the supplementaries last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister bring in the actual expenditures in the last fiscal year on comparable items?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, if there are any.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
